record.paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
record.original_question: Can peer-to-peer protocols be designed so that they do not introduce new amplification mechanisms or back-door communication channels that attackers can exploit to scale and coordinate denial-of-service attacks?

evidence.quote: It is important to design future P2P protocols such that they do not open up new opportunities for attackers to use as amplifiers and back-door communication channels.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a peer-to-peer (P2P) overlay network: a distributed system in which autonomous nodes (peers) communicate directly with one another over an underlying packet-switched network (such as the Internet) to share data, route lookups, and forward messages, without relying on a fixed centralized server. A P2P protocol specifies (i) how peers join and leave the overlay, (ii) how they discover and maintain connections to other peers, (iii) how queries, requests, and responses are forwarded, and (iv) how data is published, located, and retrieved.

For such a protocol, define the following adversarial notions:

1. An amplification mechanism is any protocol feature that allows an attacker who sends a request of size s (in bytes, or in number of packets) and consumes effort e (CPU, bandwidth, or state) to cause one or more honest peers, or the protocol as a whole, to generate aggregate traffic of size S ≫ s or effort E ≫ e directed at a target chosen by the attacker. The amplification factor is the ratio S/s (or E/e). A protocol is said to introduce a new amplification mechanism (relative to the bare underlying network) if there exists an attacker strategy whose amplification factor, when measured against a chosen victim (which may be a peer, a non-participant host, or a network link), is strictly larger than what the same attacker could achieve by direct use of the underlying network.

2. A back-door communication channel is any protocol-induced capability that enables an attacker to relay, indirect, or coordinate messages among compromised or colluding nodes (or to reach a victim) in a way that is not available, or is significantly harder to achieve, using the underlying network alone. This includes using overlay routing, caches, or forwarding rules to obscure the origin of attack traffic, to synchronize distributed attackers, or to bypass network-level filtering.

A denial-of-service (DoS) attack against a target T is any attacker strategy that renders T (a peer, a host outside the overlay, or a network resource) unable to provide its normal service to legitimate users for a sustained period.

Problem. Design a P2P protocol Π satisfying the following properties simultaneously, or prove that no such protocol exists:

(a) Functionality: Π supports the standard primitives of a data-sharing P2P system, namely peer join/leave, peer discovery, key-based lookup, and data publication/retrieval, with performance (latency, lookup cost, maintenance overhead) within a constant factor of known efficient overlays.

(b) No new amplification: There exists a constant c ≥ 1 such that for every polynomial-time adversary controlling any constant fraction of peers and any chosen victim T, the amplification factor obtainable via Π (in bandwidth and in computational effort) is at most c. In particular, Π must not enable amplification factors that grow with the size of the overlay.

(c) No back-door channels: For every polynomial-time adversary, any covert relaying, indirection, or coordination capability obtainable through Π can be simulated, up to polynomial overhead, by an adversary with only direct access to the underlying network; equivalently, Π provides no protocol-level capability that materially assists an attacker in scaling or coordinating a DoS attack beyond what is possible at the network layer.

(d) Robustness: Properties (b) and (c) must hold under realistic adversarial conditions, including Sybil identities, churn, and partial compromise of peers.

Either exhibit a concrete protocol Π meeting (a)–(d) together with a rigorous proof of (b)–(d), or establish an impossibility result showing that any protocol satisfying (a) must violate (b), (c), or (d).
artifact.status_search_result: The question of designing P2P protocols that avoid introducing amplification vectors and covert relaying/coordination channels usable for DoS remains an active and unresolved research direction. Surveys on P2P DoS/DDoS and amplification (e.g., DNS, Memcached, BitTorrent DHT, and structured overlay amplification studies) continue to report new amplification vectors in deployed overlays, and no general protocol or impossibility result is known that settles the question in the form posed. Hence the problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Amplification and DRDoS Attack Defense – A Survey and New Perspectives
status_evidence.snippet: Survey documents continually discovered amplification vectors in distributed and P2P protocols.
status_evidence.claim: New amplification mechanisms in distributed/P2P protocols continue to be discovered, indicating the design problem is unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Exploiting the Bitcoin P2P network as an amplifier
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work demonstrates novel amplification and coordination channels in deployed P2P systems.
status_evidence.claim: Recent deployed P2P systems still exhibit new amplification and back-door channels usable by attackers.
